title: The Internet’s Encryption Is Being Rewired Before Quantum Computers Arrive

lines.text: Post quantum security isn't really a cipher problem.
lines.label: CLAIM

lines.text: It's an inventory problem, and that changes where you start.
lines.label: CLAIM

lines.text: Think about the lock on an ordinary shopping website.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: Before your browser trusts that site, it checks a certificate,
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: and that certificate leans on public key encryption underneath.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: But it's rarely just one certificate.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: The site might use several, and the payment service behind it
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: can connect through another dependency you never see.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: A private network tunnel can rely on the same technology,
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: a software update can carry a signature from another system,
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: and the device receiving that update might be years old.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: So every connection becomes one more place to inspect.
lines.label: PROOF

lines.text: That's why swapping out one library can't finish the job.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: The hard part isn't the new math, it's finding the whole chain.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Now, here's the threat itself.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Future quantum computers could weaken the public key systems we rely on,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: which is why post quantum algorithms were designed to resist them.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: The standards for the main replacements already exist.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: But an algorithm can't protect a system nobody can find.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: So where do you start? With a list.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Write down every place public key encryption appears,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: which algorithm sits behind each lock and certificate,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: which software calls each cryptographic function,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: what data each system is protecting,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and which vendors stand between your systems and your users.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Then rank everything by how sensitive it is
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and how hard it would be to replace.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Secrets that need to last for years come before short lived messages,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and critical services come before convenient internal tools.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: If that sounds familiar, it should.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: It's the same rule behind ordinary software maintenance.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: A web certificate is one place cryptography hides.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: A network tunnel is another, a device update signature is a third,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and a software library can quietly hide a fourth.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: In every case, compatibility matters as much as encryption.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: The new algorithm has to work on real devices,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: in real browsers and servers,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: with certificates issued by real vendors,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and it has to survive testing under normal business traffic.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Because a replacement that breaks your customers isn't ready.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: In other words, migration is a software and business project.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Security, engineering, purchasing and your vendors all have to coordinate.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: You test before you touch production,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: you keep a record after every replacement,
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: and you avoid hard coding one algorithm forever.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: That ability has a name, crypto agility.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: It means you can change algorithms without rebuilding everything.
lines.label: PATTERN

lines.text: Now here's what happens if you skip the inventory.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: Hidden systems turn into blockers right when you need to move.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: A certificate expires before anyone finds its owner.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: A vendor needs changes before your team can even respond.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: An old device rejects the new connection,
lines.label: COST

lines.text: and suddenly software updates stop reaching your customers.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: An emergency replacement means rushed testing and expensive outages,
lines.label: COST

lines.text: and when one dependency serves many products, the damage spreads.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: Security teams end up searching in the middle of the crisis,
lines.label: COST

lines.text: business leaders find the risk buried in ordinary contracts,
lines.label: COST

lines.text: and customers feel it the only way they can, as broken trust.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: So the cost isn't just stronger encryption.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: It's people, testing, vendors and downtime,
lines.label: COST

lines.text: and every month you wait makes each hidden dependency harder to schedule.
lines.label: COST

lines.text: So remember this. Quantum readiness begins with knowing your locks.
lines.label: REFRAME

lines.text: Then you replace vulnerable algorithms one dependency at a time,
lines.label: REFRAME

lines.text: test every connection before you call it done,
lines.label: REFRAME

lines.text: and build systems that can change again without panic.
lines.label: REFRAME

lines.text: Here's something you can do this week.
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: Pick one important service and map it.
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: List its certificates, libraries, vendors and data flows,
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: ask which public key algorithm each connection uses,
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: and mark the one dependency nobody has tested yet.
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: Give that gap an owner and a test plan.
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: That small map turns a distant threat into real work.
lines.label: CTA

lines.text: Because post quantum security was never a cipher problem.
lines.label: CTA
